subject: english-literature
title: Big Ideas, Small Places
welcome_lead: From a tiny garden, a whole theme can bloom.
meta_desc: KS3 English Literature adventure on themes emerging through setting.
final_note: You can now link a setting to the theme it serves.

concepts.def: When place acts on the plot.
Wide world or era around events.

walkthroughs.body_html: Love, loss, courage and justice are universal themes — readers across cultures recognise them.
In some stories, a forest or sea behaves like a character — opposing or helping the hero. That's setting as character.
The macro setting might be 'wartime London'. The microsetting could be 'a damp Anderson shelter'. Both shape theme.

mcqs.q: What is the structural framework of The Canterbury Tales?
options: It is a religious text used in Catholic services.
It is one continuous story told by Chaucer from beginning to end.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
A frame narrative — pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell stories along the way, allowing Chaucer to juxtapose different voices, genres and social classes.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a metaphor and a simile?
options: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing IS another, making an implicit comparison without those connectives.
A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
Metaphors are short and similes are long.

mcqs.q: What is the dramatic function of a soliloquy?
options: A soliloquy is any long speech a character gives.
It reveals a character's inner thoughts directly to the audience while the character is alone on stage — a convention granting access to private psychology.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
